image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Two-panel line chart**
  - **Graph A:** multi-series **step line chart** showing **net change in retail jobs**
  - **Graph B:** multi-series **line chart** showing **percentage change in retail jobs**

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses **vertical faceting / stacked panels**: Graph A and Graph B are separate panels for two different measures.
- Within each panel, there are **multiple overlaid series**.
- No bar stacking; not a small-multiples grid.
- Uses **direct labeling** of selected lines and de-emphasized background lines for “other retail sectors.”

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year (’02–’16) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Net change in retail jobs | Quantitative | Position on y-axis in **Graph A** |
| Percentage change in retail jobs | Quantitative | Position on y-axis in **Graph B** |
| Retail sector / industry category (e.g., E-commerce, Department stores, Warehouse clubs and other, Total retail industry, 25 other retail sectors) | Categorical/nominal | Line color/hue, line identity, direct text labels |
| Zero baseline | Quantitative reference value | Horizontal reference line at y = 0 |

comments.raw_comment: I can see that E-commerce is currently a booming industry within retail, and this stands out amongst the other forms of retail. While other forms of retail, including department stores and warehouse clubs, have remained largely the same in percentage change in jobs (graph B), E-commerce has been shooting up over the last decade and a half. It's especially interesting to see that the overall retail industry was vacillating between high and low points (graph A), but again, E-commerce remained steady. I wonder the underlying causes of the steady decline of department stores, in particular. E-commerce is an extremely fast and convenient way to shop, but I had no idea that it was this much stronger than other forms of retail. Overall, these graphs prove the common theme that our world is becoming increasingly technology-based and the new innovations that have arisen through this new world approach have far-reaching influences on our lives. Society is steadily shifting towards online commerce.

If the second graph is any indication, the retail industry isn't changing; it's the scope of it and the means of it that are changing its very definition. With that being said, I wonder how the continued growth of warehouse clubs can be explained; while not contradicting the observation of an increasing turn towards e-commerce, its continued survival raises some questions about the overall retail landscape.

comments.raw_comment: I can see that E-commerce is currently a booming industry within retail, and this stands out amongst the other forms of retail. While other forms of retail, including department stores and warehouse clubs, have remained largely the same in percentage change in jobs (graph B), E-commerce has been shooting up over the last decade and a half. It's especially interesting to see that the overall retail industry was vacillating between high and low points (graph A), but again, E-commerce remained steady. I wonder the underlying causes of the steady decline of department stores, in particular. E-commerce is an extremely fast and convenient way to shop, but I had no idea that it was this much stronger than other forms of retail. Overall, these graphs prove the common theme that our world is becoming increasingly technology-based and the new innovations that have arisen through this new world approach have far-reaching influences on our lives. Society is steadily shifting towards online commerce.

I notice that the warehouse clubs had more jobs offered than the other commerce. E-commerce is the second most at offering jobs while department stores job offering declined. The total retail industry has increased from 2002 to 2008, but decreased until 2010. After 2010, the  job offerings increased rapidly increased. The other graph shows the percentage of job offering that each group offered over the 15 years. Although, e-commerce does not offer the most amount of jobs, it's percentage increased the most from 0 to 300% within the last fifteen years. Not only do the people prefer to have better salary, warehouses, clubs and e-commerce require more people. Today, more people want to everything online, because it's cheaper, faster, and easier. That's why e-commerce has increased the most out of all other companies. I think e-commerce will eventually overtake warehouse/clubs employment, because of its rapid exponential progression.

These two different graphs show the transformation of retail jobs and department stores from 2002 to 2016. However, graph A reveals the net change of the jobs and stores, while graph B depicts the percentage change. The scales (y-axis) of the graphs are quite different, thus a clear comparison with distinct numbers will be unlikely.

In graph A, the decrease is over 500 in some areas; while the graph B shows a general decrease a general of less than 100. Graph A shows a gradually increase of e- commerce, while graph B shows a faster one within the time frame. The large scale of graph A makes it very hard to decide how much the e- commerce has risen, while graph B shows a 300 increase.
There is a rise in the total retail industry on both graphs, but there is a very slight increase seen on graph B. The increase of the total industry of graph A was seen with a rise over 500,000. The same idea is presented in the rise of warehouse clubs and others.
These results are in response of new technology that allows one to buy ideas online much easier. I also believe that there is a need for jobs to be filled in existing department stores, before new one are built.

comments.raw_comment:
Both graphs illustrate the same general information, but Graph A depicts it via net change, using money by the thousands, which Graph B illustrates the percent change. This means that, while the data is the same, the depiction is wildly different; for instance, I notice that although warehouse clubs account for the largest amount of net chanege on the first graph, the percentage growth of e-commerce far exceeds that (even if it had less of a net change).

The story that these graphs are telling points to the increasingly shifting tides of retail as it orients away from department stores and more towards e-commerce. If the second graph is any indication, the retail industry isn't changing; it's the scope of it and the means of it that are changing its very definition. With that being said, I wonder how the continued growth of warehouse clubs can be explained; while not contradicting the observation of an increasing turn towards e-commerce, its continued survival raises some questions about the overall retail landscape.

comments.raw_comment: The first graph shows the net change in retail jobs over the last 15 years, while the second graph shows the percent change in retail jobs over the last 15 years. You can see in first graph, net change, that there is a large growth in warehouse jobs and as a result of this increase there is a decrease in department store jobs. In the second chart, percent change, it is clear that the number of people that hold a job in the E-commerce area is increasing. It can be inferred that this is due to the increased use and dependence that society has begun to have on the internet. It is easier and more convenient for people to work online, because they can choose their hours and work from anywhere. E-commerce jobs are also easy to get and there are more opportunities available. You can work for yourself or other companies, even set up your own business.

I wonder if this was due to skepticism among the participants.

The first graph shows a change in retail jobs over the last 15 years, starting from 2002, while the second graph shows the change in percentage of retail jobs in the same sectors. The different industries shown are Department stores, E-commerce, and Warehouse Clubs and other. This information could be found by doing research in the different fields and calculating total revenue earned by a single industry annually.

I noticed the increase in net change of total retail jobs since 2010, shown in graph A. In graph B, there is a very large percentage change in online or e-commerce retail jobs; however, the total retail industry does not significantly change. The graph only shows the three main variables of E-commerce, Warehouse clubs, and Department stores, but it also includes "25 other retail sectors" . The absence of these other sectors puts E-commerce, Warehouse clubs, and Department stores in direct comparison with each other. 

When analyzing the graphs, I thought the selection of which sectors to include was interesting. These three sectors are the main industries that people think about in retail. Seeing the rise in online retail jobs, I wonder how many other industries see this same increase, and if any industries actually experience a decrease in online occupation opportunities. 

This graph explains the decrease in department stores' marks on the retail industry, and online/warehouse jobs rising in its place. Graph B shows the total retail industry keeping a constant, with no significant percent change. This is evidence that the rise in e-commerce and warehouse clubs are increasingly taking the place of department stores, as well as the 25 other retail sectors that are all decreasing in percentage. By itself, department stores do not account for all of the decrease in the retail industry. There are actually many more sectors that are also losing their places to e-commerce.

I noticed that in both graphs, there is a boom in the total number of jobs in the retail industry starting in 2012. There seems to be a correlation between the number of e-commerce jobs and total retail jobs because of a rapid growth in e-commerce, despite warehouse club jobs increasing at a steady rate. I wonder if said decline in department store jobs, as well as the decline in the net percent growth of the 25 other retail sectors, has to do with the growing popularity and accessibility of the e-commerce industry. This seems to be partly due to the notion that when it comes to purchasing in bulk, there is a level of trust gained from purchasing packs of water or a large piece of furniture in person, rather than online where you cannot physically check for deficiencies on a larger scale.

Looking at both the net and percentage change in retail jobs in the past 15 years, the most prominent feature is the positive slopes of E-commerce and Warehouse clubs/other jobs. It is clear that these positions are much more popular today than they were in 2002. I also notice the declining slope of department store jobs, indicating their decrease in popularity. Overall, the total retail industry has seen an increase since 2002, but has experienced intermittent decline (for example, in 2008 we see the slope plummet exponentially, likely due to the stock market crash of 2008). 

I can infer that the increasing number of retail positions in Ecommerce and Warehouse clubs is because of their increased utilization and popularity. Both online and in large stores, wide varieties of merchandise are available, easily accessible, and much cheaper than in department stores, making them the sought after option. Because online shopping and warehouse stores receive many customers and transactions, they require larger staffs to satisfy the needs of the store. The more successful they are, the more chains can be opened, hence increasing the workforce even further.  The recent unpopularity of department stores is likely due to people turning to these cheaper alternatives; hence, the more ecommerce and warehouse clubs dominate the retail industry, the more department store shopping will decline. Less traffic in department stores requires less staffing, and therefore, fewer jobs.

comments.raw_comment:
Thanks to all teachers and students who responded during this very busy time before vacation.  Did the graph make you want to shop for presents?

Many noticed that Graph A is the net change in jobs and Graph B is the percentage change.  Could you see how the net change was reflected in the percentage?  I think we were not surprised by the large increase in e-commerce jobs and corresponding large decrease in department store jobs.  But, we wondered whether this has affected sales.   And many wondered about the Warehouse graph. How did that coincide with the e-commerce jobs? Is there a connection between the two? Do we buy more or less with e-commerce?  What’s the future for retail jobs and sales? So many questions to consider.

Since we continue to post responses, whenever they arrive, is there more that you notice?  More that you wonder?  Talk to your classmates and even read the moderators’ responses.  Maybe something they say will lead to more things you notice, wonder, and conjecture.     

Remember to check back on Friday, December 15 to learn more about these graphs -- and we hope to see you again next month on Tuesday, January 9 (always the second Tuesday of the month) for our next "What's Going On In This Graph?"   Signing off now -- Sharon in Boston and Paul in Washington, DC.  See you next year!

Welcome to What’s Going On in This Graph?.  It’s December and many of us are buying gifts for the holidays.  Are you buying in stores or are you buying online – e-commerce?  These graphs tell a story about how our buying habits are changing.   

What do you NOTICE? What may this imply?

What do you WONDER? Where could you find the answers to what you wonder?

What’s GOING ON in these graphs?  What can you infer that is beyond what the graphs show directly?

The questions are intended to build on one another, so try to answer them in order.  Start with “I notice” and then “I wonder,” and end with “The story this graph tells is ….”

This month, we have two graphs.  Think about relating the graphs to each other to gain more insights.

Wouldn’t you love to hear what other students have to say about your response?  Read some responses.  Then, press "Reply" to an interesting response to get a discussion going.

We look forward to reading your discoveries.

I notice on Graph A that Warehouse clubs and other had the most net change retail jobs over the last 15 years. The reasons are endless for the big net change. Also, the retail industry has the second net change in retail jobs over the last 15 years. This may be because of the rise of the industry this time of year. I notice on Graph B that E-commerce has the most percentage change in retail jobs over the last 15 years this may be because jobs are needed in their warehouses and other shifts in the company.
I wonder why the e-commerce has the least positive change over the last 15 years. I would expect that it would be the most because of the rise of Amazon, and many other e-commerce companies. I also wonder why the total retail industry is rising. Maybe as the population of the world increases, the need for clothes increasing. Maybe in the near future the retail industry will move to e-commerce but, I believe that trying and buying clothes will still be something to watch for in the future.
The story these graphs are telling us is the decline of regular department and the rise of e-commerce and online shopping, shown in both Graph A and B. Jobs that used to be in Department stores have shifted to e-commerce. This graph was justified by Black Friday where online shopping sharply rose.  This is what's going on in this graph.
